item.title: House speaker's wife ministers to Hill staffers, but nonprofit funding is a mystery
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
After House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana) ascended to one of the most powerful offices in Washington three years ago, his wife, a faith-based counselor, turned her focus to the nation’s capital. Kelly Johnson reoriented a religious nonprofit she was running back home in the Shreveport area into a ministry focused on female congressional staffers. Its new purpose, according to an IRS filing, was to help “the hundreds of unreached young women” working around Capitol Hill “find purpose, belonging, and Christian community.” Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Through the organization, a part-time endeavor run solely by Johnson, she provides counseling, delivers speeches and conducts “spiritual heritage tours” of the U.S. Capitol that highlight the nation’s Christian history. In 2024, financial disclosures show Johnson was paid $50,000 for 10 hours of work per week. The nonprofit, Onward Christian Education Services, has become part of the rising presence in official Washington of evangelical Christianity as its devotees, a key bloc of support for President Donald Trump, seek to inject a biblical worldview into American politics and government. The centerpiece of Johnson’s organization is the faith-based counseling that she said she provides free to staff and the spouses of House members. “I’m a missionary here,” Johnson said in an interview. “It’s kind of a calling in this life for me,” she added. “This is what I love to do. This is my heart.” The full extent of Kelly Johnson’s work in Washington is unclear, however. Some mysteries remain about her organization, including who is funding it. Onward Christian Education Services brought in an average of more than $60,000 in contributions annually during its early years. Donors are disclosed to the IRS but redacted in publicly available filings. Johnson said her nonprofit has “several large benefactors,” whom she described as “primarily just individuals who have an interest in this and have a heart in this.” She would not name them or disclose whether they are also supporters of her husband’s political campaigns, and she declined to voluntarily provide unredacted filings to The Washington Post. The publicly available records contain inconsistencies and omissions. Johnson, who IRS filings indicate also does the bookkeeping, has occasionally revised annual revenue figures for previous years without explanation. On a 2023 annual form, she neglected to report her own salary, which accounts for almost 90 percent of spending since the organization formed. The Post spoke to four people who work on nonprofit law and government ethics. They stressed there’s nothing wrong with the purpose of Onward Christian Education Services but raised concerns about how Kelly Johnson’s close connection to the speaker’s office could benefit the nonprofit. “It should make everyone uncomfortable that the speaker’s wife would be raising money for a mission to serve congressional staff,” said Meredith McGehee, a former lobbyist for several nonpartisan groups that advocate for campaign finance transparency and anti-corruption measures in government. “It really dances on that blurred line of separation of church and state and using public resources for private interests.” In a statement, Mike Johnson praised his wife’s ministry work and Christian counseling services as life-changing for many. “She has a true gift with people and has inspired many other women to live out their faith, overcome their obstacles, and find peace and success, even in an environment as challenging as Capitol Hill,” he said. Kelly Johnson has intentionally tried to keep her nonprofit’s second chapter out of the spotlight after what she considered an unfairly hostile reception to the couple’s religious views when Mike Johnson became speaker in October 2023. Onward Christian Education Services previously operated for five years in Louisiana. The Post discovered the change in mission when a reporter requested recent IRS filings for the group, which had not filed legally required disclosures for tax-exempt organizations for two years. Kelly Johnson submitted the organization’s 2024 filing after the inquiry, revealing its new purpose, though she did not explain the delay. A spokesperson said Johnson requested an extension for her 2025 IRS filing and has not yet completed it. The form is typically due in May and nonprofits can ask for a six-month extension. After an initial interview, Johnson declined to speak to a reporter again. The Post has pieced together this portrait of Onward Christian Education Services through that conversation, an analysis of available public documents and written questions submitted to Mike Johnson’s office. The Johnsons were ordained as Southern Baptist missionaries more than two decades ago, and in 2017, their church in Benton, Louisiana, formally ordained Kelly Johnson as a minister. The same year, she was licensed as a pastoral counselor through the National Christian Counselors Association, opening a practice at the church. Though she has never held elected office herself, Johnson has also long been politically active. Two decades ago, when Mike Johnson was still a practicing attorney, the couple were vocal advocates for covenant marriage, a legal union with more limited standing for divorce, and participated in an interview with Diane Sawyer about their experience. Kelly Johnson has previously worked for Louisiana Right to Life, an antiabortion advocacy group. She was intimately involved in her husband’s political rise. In 2022, the couple started a podcast together covering “hot topics and current events from a Christian perspective,” which they hosted until Mike Johnson became speaker. Onward Christian Education Services was created as a tax-exempt organization in April 2019 to counter what the Johnsons described at the time as cultural attacks against people of faith and the traditional family. Kelly Johnson recently told The Post she came to see that education was important. “People have forgotten our history and our Christian heritage,” she said. “For a long time, I felt that burden.” The purpose of the nonprofit, according to early tax filings, was to “empower Christians to follow the Biblical commands to understand and meet the challenges of our day,” primarily through live seminars at churches across Louisiana and eventually other states. Kelly Johnson served as the CEO and the only employee. “Mike and Kelly Johnson ‘rang the bell’ to awaken our people to become Christian patriots,” Gevan Spinney, a local pastor who serves as president of Onward Christian Education Services’ board, told the Baptist Message, a faith-based publication, in an article that May touting the seminar. Onward Christian Education Services initially did not submit any filings to the IRS. In 2022, when Kelly Johnson submitted forms for the first three years of operation, she blamed “a communication gap and misunderstanding of the filing requirements” for a nonprofit so closely affiliated with a religious denomination. The organization paid $6,475 in penalties to the Treasury Department. From 2019 to 2023, Johnson reported working 10 hours a week for Onward Christian Education Services, earning between $35,383 and $64,485 annually. During the covid-19 pandemic, the organization developed prerecorded presentations of its seminars. The Johnsons’ podcast followed. Once her husband became speaker, Kelly Johnson said, the couple had to spend more time in Washington and were no longer able to conduct regular church visits. So in 2024, she transitioned the focus of her nonprofit to the capital, folding in her counseling business and offering free sessions. Johnson said she has 10 or 11 clients, whom she counsels through a lens of spirituality and the Bible about the issues that women face, including anxiety and depression, adjusting to a new city and problems with their families. The organization maintains a low profile because, Johnson said, she fears for her safety. Her clients come through word of mouth, rather than advertising, Johnson said, and unlike in Louisiana, where she had an office at her church, they meet for counseling sessions at home or over FaceTime. “People want things to be private,” she said. “If I had an office, there would likely be protesters outside of it. I would like to have an office. Boy, would I like to.” Taylor Haulsee, a spokesman for Mike Johnson, said in a statement that “no House Republican Caucus or member office has ever been used for” outreach to staffers and that most of the nonprofit’s activities take place away from the Capitol complex. Other programming since Onward Christian Education Services shifted to Washington has included Kelly Johnson speaking at a Christian women’s conference in Kentucky in 2024, leading the spiritual heritage tours of the Capitol and organizing a Bible study, which Johnson said was hard to maintain because “people are just so overcommitted.” Johnson turned down a request from The Post for one of her Capitol tours. Haulsee said the tours are within House guidelines and they are “scheduled for small groups of people upon request, which is the same access available to any and all citizens to the People’s House.” He would not share who those people are or what they visit on the tours. As she expanded her ministry into Washington, Johnson teamed up with “like-minded organizations operating in the nation’s capital such as Concerned Women for America, Inc.,” according to the 2024 IRS filing. Concerned Women for America is an advocacy group “dedicated to impacting the culture for Christ through education and public policy,” according to its website. A spokesperson declined to answer questions about the organization’s work with Johnson. Government ethics advocates said the lack of transparency surrounding Onward Christian Education Services means the public cannot be certain whether donors are using the organization to gain access to the Johnsons or whether Kelly Johnson receives advantages, such as access to the Capitol for her tours, that other nonprofits could not get. “Is it serving a political purpose or is it serving an actual charity?” said Philip Hackney, a professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Law who specializes in nonprofit law. Without proper safeguards, young staffers could also feel pressured to participate in Johnson’s counseling and Bible study, said Davina Hurt, director of the government ethics program at Santa Clara University’s Markkula Center for Applied Ethics. She said it would be helpful to know who extends the invitations, whether the speaker’s name gets invoked and whether attendance is ever shared with the boss of a Hill staffer. “The institutional concern one should have is the power that’s present in those situations,” Hurt said. “If you want to advance through the ranks, you will feel pressure to some degree.” Haulsee said no staffers have ever been pressured to participate in Johnson’s programming. McGehee, the former ethics lobbyist, said she is sympathetic to the challenges a prominent politician’s spouse faces figuring out an appropriate role in Washington. But Onward Christian Education Services should at least articulate a firmer wall between Johnson and the money, she said, to avoid even the appearance of conflicts of interest. McGehee questioned why Johnson needed to be paid at all to minister to congressional staffers. “This is not about the value of the work,” McGehee said. “But it’s fraught.” In 2024, an IRS filing shows that Johnson took a salary of $50,000 even though the organization brought in no revenue that year, depleting its reserves to $5,797. Johnson said she was too busy with her husband’s new position to fundraise. The 2024 filing is the most recent financial statement available. Johnson deferred to her four-member board on questions about her salary. Three of its members, who have all been in their positions since Onward Christian Education Services began, did not respond to attempts by The Post to speak with them. Board Secretary Julianna Parks, an attorney and local government official in Bossier Parish, Louisiana, said they set Johnson’s salary annually by looking at what other nonprofit directors in the area make. The Johnsons “insisted that it not be excessive in any way,” she said. “So we always erred on the lower side.” Parks said she first met Mike Johnson professionally through the local law community and became friendly with the Johnsons when their children attended the same private Christian school. She declined to discuss any other specifics of the organization or how the board operates, including whether it had advised Kelly Johnson as she refocused her work to Washington. “I don’t really feel comfortable answering specifically to this organization,” Parks said. She said that she thought a story about Onward Christian Education Services was a bad idea because she did not want to put a spotlight on the Johnson family during a dangerous time in the country. item.title: Abortion, voter ID and more: These ballot measures could reshape state laws
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The battle for control of Congress is getting the lion's share of the attention in the lead-up to the midterms, but there are a lot of other consequential measures that'll appear on ballots this November that could have a direct impact on voters' lives. Ballot measures often don't receive much national attention, but every two years, voters across the country decide whether to adopt policies that have major implications for their states. This year is no different. There are more than 140 total measures collectively across 40 states this year. Many touch on some of the biggest issues in U.S. politics, including abortion, transgender rights, voting and the democratic process itself. Ballot measures can give the people a way to directly alter the laws in their states instead of relying solely on their elected representatives to create policy on their behalf. In some cases, they provide an opportunity for voters to endorse or reject something their state legislature wants to do. In other cases, regular citizens can get their preferred policy on the ballot directly through a signature-gathering campaign. Here's a rundown of some of the major measures on statewide ballots this year. Abortion The Supreme Court's 2022 decision to overturn the nationwide abortion protections established by Roe v. Wade instantly turned abortion access into a state-by-state issue. It also led to a flurry of ballot measures across the country in which voters were asked to decide whether their states should protect or restrict abortion rights. In the years since, voters have generally come down in favor of protecting abortion rights. Yahoo That trend will get another test this year due to abortion-related measures in four states. In Idaho , voters will decide whether to overturn their state's strict abortion restrictions and establish a right to reproductive freedom and privacy, including abortion until fetal viability. If the measure passes, Idaho will become the latest red state where voters have used a ballot initiative to expand abortion rights. One of those red states is Missouri , where voters approved a measure in 2024 that struck down some of the nation's most restrictive abortion laws. A Republican-backed measure on this year's ballot would repeal that 2024 amendment and allow strict abortion restrictions to be put back into place. The same measure would also create new limits on gender-affirming care in the state. Two other states that already have relatively permissive laws around abortion access — Nevada and Virginia — are voting on measures that would enshrine abortion rights in their state constitutions, a step that would make it much harder to restrict access in the future. Transgender policy The debate over transgender rights, particularly when it comes to minors, has become a central issue in American politics. It should be no surprise, then, that a number of states have measures related to the topic on the ballot this year. All of them would impose new limits on transgender rights. Four states — Washington , Nebraska , Arizona and Colorado — will vote on measures that would ban trans athletes from participating on sports teams that match their gender identity. There are some important differences from state to state, though. The proposals in Washington and Nebraska would only apply to girls' and women's teams. Colorado's and Arizona's would apply to both male and female teams. Washington's bill also includes a stipulation that would require all K-12 students, whether they identify as trans or not, who want to play girls' or women's sports to have their sex verified by a doctor . Arizona's measure would also ban schools from allowing trans minors or adults to access bathrooms, locker rooms or other private spaces designated for a sex that doesn't match the one they were assigned at birth. A separate initiative in Colorado would ban gender-affirming surgeries for minors. Missouri's measure would go even further. In addition to banning the surgeries, it would also prohibit minors from receiving other forms of gender-affirming care, like hormone therapy and puberty blockers. Voter ID Six states will vote on measures related to voter ID. Those in California, Colorado and Nevada would either establish or expand laws requiring voters to show ID when they cast their ballots. Each of the proposals would also require voter ID for mail-in ballots. Arizona, Ohio and North Carolina already have strict voter ID requirements in place under state law, but measures in each state would add or expand those requirements in their state constitutions. Schools Schools have been a major flash point for culture war battles in recent years. A handful of measures on the ballot in November will ask voters to weigh in on some of those debates. Arizona and Wisconsin both have measures that would ban affirmative action in schools and all other government agencies. Alabama has a pair of proposals. One would require public schools to play the national anthem at least once a week. The other would make the recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance a daily requirement and mandate school boards to adopt policies that allow student-led prayer. Fuse via Getty Images A sweeping parental rights initiative in Washington would give parents of public school students substantially more oversight over the education their children receive, including the power to review curricula and textbooks. It would also put strict new limits on the kinds of medical care schools can provide without parental notification and roll back changes to the state's parental rights law that protected against discrimination and bullying in schools. The ballot initiative process Ballot measures frequently center on contentious political issues, but in recent years, the initiative process itself has increasingly become the subject of political debate. Five states will vote on measures that would make it harder for citizen-led ballot initiatives to become law. They would accomplish that by either raising the share of the vote certain measures need to get approved or restricting the subjects that initiatives can address. Voters in California and Utah will consider measures that would require certain initiatives that would raise taxes to receive more than the simple majority of support they currently need to be successful. California's would raise the bar for voter-proposed local special taxes to two-thirds of the vote. Utah's would set the new standard for tax-related citizen initiatives at 60%. North Dakota and South Dakota both have measures that would require any attempt to change their state constitutions to get 60% of the vote. Voters cast their ballots at a polling location inside the Candia Youth Athletic Association during a primary election in Candia, N.H. Mel Musto/Bloomberg via Getty Images Changing the threshold for success by 10 percentage points may not sound like a huge deal, but it is often the difference between a proposal becoming law and being rejected. For example, initiatives in Florida that would have legalized abortion and recreational marijuana use both received majority support from voters in 2024, but neither became law because they fell short of the state's 60% approval standard. Idaho has a measure on the ballot that would ban initiatives aimed at legalizing marijuana, psychedelics and other narcotics. If it passes, only the state legislature would have the power to legalize or decriminalize those substances. Another two states will decide on measures designed to protect the initiative process. A proposal in Montana would amend the state's constitution to guarantee citizens' rights to pursue ballot initiatives and make it harder for the government to interfere with measures approved by voters. In Missouri , voters will weigh in on a measure that would prohibit the state's Republican-led legislature from weakening the initiative process. It would also bar it from amending or repealing any measures that have passed unless 80% of both chambers agree to put the change before voters. Other notable initiatives There are many pivotal ballot initiatives being considered across the country that don't fit neatly into a specific category. Here are a few of them. Alaska voters will decide whether to repeal their state's recently adopted ranked-choice voting system. A proposal in Arizona would ban new traffic cameras without direct voter approval. Nebraska will choose whether to legalize online sports betting . Vermont will consider a measure that would ban discrimination based on gender identity. Virginia will decide if people convicted of felonies should have their right to vote restored once they're released from prison. A measure in Wisconsin would prohibit the government from closing places of worship during public health emergencies. Massachusetts will consider whether recreational marijuana sales should once again be made illegal. A proposal on the ballot in North Dakota would require all public schools to provide free breakfast and lunch. Lower-stakes — but still noteworthy — measures under consideration include a Colorado initiative that would enshrine the right to hunt and fish in the state constitution and a request for Idaho voters to select an official state gun . item.title: Some peptide users report lasting symptoms as RFK Jr. pushes for wider access
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
After the third day of squirting an experimental drug up his nose, Dylan Meetze felt horrible. "It was like I was underwater, like it took the most to do anything," he said. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Meetze stopped taking the drug, but he endured fatigue and anxiety for months afterward, and his eyes and muscles twitched, he said. He had taken BPC-157, a peptide drug popularized by podcasts about wellness, longevity and what's called "body optimization." Peptide is a general term for substances that are smaller than proteins but composed of the same building blocks. Dozens of peptide drugs, including insulin and GLP-1 weight loss medicines, have garnered approval by the Food and Drug Administration. But BPC-157 and many others have not because they haven't undergone clinical trials. This fact hasn't stopped online influencers from promoting them as remedies for muscle injuries, gut issues, covid and more. Use of BPC-157 is growing in the United States, particularly among White males, according to a new analysis of millions of de-identified electronic health records. Since 2020, the analysis, which hasn't yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal, found that more than 1,000 people told doctors they had used the drug. Meetze said he decided to take BPC-157 after listening to Andrew Huberman, a Stanford neuroscientist with more than 16 million followers on YouTube, Instagram and TikTok, who talks up peptides frequently on his podcasts. Studies in mice suggest that BPC-157 helps muscles heal and has "very high safety profiles," Huberman has said, "at least, with respect to the lethal dosing." His guest on one episode, Craig Koniver, a doctor who sells peptides through his wellness clinic, called BPC-157 "super safe" and recommended it for "anyone who's working out on a regular basis." Koniver did not respond to requests for comment. Huberman didn't respond to multiple queries from KFF Health News, but an automatic reply linked to a disclaimer on his Huberman Lab website that says the podcast doesn't constitute medical advice: "Any reliance on information provided through the podcast is solely at the user's own risk." Hoping BPC-157 might help him advance as a weightlifter, Meetze said he bought the drug last year from an online vendor, Researchem. A chemical supply company with that name sells experimental peptides through its website, warning that the substances are "solely for laboratory research" and are "not intended for human consumption." (It lists an address in Hillsboro, Oregon, that corresponds to a shared office space. A receptionist at the space said Researchem wasn't registered there, and multiple queries from KFF Health News to the email address listed on the website went unanswered.) Companies are required to warn that experimental peptides, which haven't been approved by the FDA, are for research use only. But many companies may soon be permitted to drop the warning because of a push by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to lower barriers to their use. He and other leaders of the Make America Healthy Again movement have promoted peptides as a way to improve the country's health. On X, before he took the helm at the Department of Health and Human Services, Kennedy vowed to end the "aggressive suppression" of "peptides, stem cells, raw milk" and "anything else that advances human health and can't be patented by Pharma." (In fact, peptides are heavily patented.) He has repeated the pledge since taking office. On Joe Rogan's podcast early this year, Kennedy said he was a "big fan" of peptides and wanted to make many of them "more accessible." On a podcast with the co-chair of the MAHA Action committee, Gary Brecka, Kennedy said the FDA's role should be to assess science, "but not tell people and not tell physicians what they can and cannot prescribe." "If you want to take an experimental drug … you ought to be able to do that," he added. This summer, Kennedy's health department appointed doctors with financial stakes in the peptide industry to a panel that advises the FDA. At an FDA meeting in July, the new appointees voted to ease restrictions on six experimental peptides, including the trendy compounds BPC-157, TB-500 and MOTS-c. They advised adding these peptides to a list, called 503A, that would allow specialized pharmacies to make the drugs for human use, even though the FDA hasn't approved them. In an email, HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard wrote that every committee member satisfies the FDA's ethics requirements. "FDA - not podcasts or politics - determines which substances qualify for inclusion on the 503A Bulks List," she wrote. The FDA has yet to issue a final decision. The vote went against FDA scientists who presented research on the six peptides, concluding there wasn't enough evidence to show that they improved any condition. Furthermore, the scientists highlighted a potential for liver damage, allergic reactions or other serious consequences. "People are saying this is about medical freedom - putting decisions back in the hands of patients," said Reshma Ramachandran, a regulatory science researcher at Yale School of Medicine. "But what we see in practice is that incentives aren't actually centered around patients. They're centered around selling products." Scientists also warned that drugmakers would be reluctant to invest millions of dollars into clinical trials on peptides if they could be sold without FDA approval. "The chances of clinical trials getting done now are diminished," said Eric Topol, executive vice president of Scripps Research, a biomedical science institute in San Diego. "We will have more people who are prey to predators that will sell, sell, sell." A lack of data leaves consumers in the dark. Meetze sought help on Reddit, where people post about pain, headaches, vision problems and a lack of motivation after taking experimental peptides. Peptide enthusiasts often comment on these posts with skepticism, attributing a person's problems to contaminated products, preexisting conditions or misuse of the drugs. The online vitriol can be intense, so Meetze welcomed an invitation to join a private group on the social platform Discord, in which people with BPC-157 side effects tried to figure out what happened to them and how to fix it. "There are millions of success stories with these peptides," Meetze said, "but no one wants to believe that this wrecks some of our lives." Reports of side effects One member of the private side-effects group, a 46-year-old software engineer named Dominik E., said he got an excruciating migraine within days of taking BPC-157 with TB-4, another unapproved peptide - a combination called the "Wolverine stack" because of its purported ability to heal wounds rapidly like its namesake Marvel superhero. "My left eye started throbbing really badly, and the left side of my face became numb," he told KFF Health News, which agreed to only partially identify him and others interviewed for this article who were concerned about divulging sensitive health information. After two months of migraines, Dominik said, the pain eased, but his face felt inflamed. "It is a total nightmare," he said. "I'm afraid how people will judge me," said Lois S., a woman who works at a Michigan elementary school. She hoped BPC-157 and another unapproved peptide, retatrutide, would help with weight loss, but she stopped taking the treatment when she felt pain. "I sought out this substance from a lab that clearly labeled it not for human use, purchased a syringe, and injected this in my kitchen," she said. "That belies all logic about what a normal person would do." Peptide proponents argue that shoddy manufacturing - not the peptides - causes harm. Therefore, they say, the FDA must protect the public by allowing doctors to prescribe peptides made for human use by pharmacies that specialize in compounding medicines. Typically, compounding pharmacies manufacture alternatives to FDA-approved drugs: for example, so that a patient can get a liquid version of a drug that the original manufacturer makes only as pills. Adding unapproved peptides to the FDA's list of compoundable drugs would mark a departure from the list's purpose, said Peter Lurie, a former FDA official who now directs the advocacy group Center for Science in the Public Interest. He said that federal and state oversight for compounding pharmacies is often lax, and the pharmacies have been cited for contamination. Furthermore, he added, the move would mislead consumers into thinking they're buying drugs backed by clinical trials. People promoting peptides often point to promising laboratory research as evidence. Rats with spinal injuries regained tail mobility after BPC-157 injections, for example, and old mice given the experimental peptide MOTS-c could run longer. On average, however, fewer than 10 percent of substances that show promise in animal studies prove effective in clinical trials. "A lot of this pseudoscience stuff sounds deeply impressive - inflammation this and telomere that - but at the end of the day, none of it really matters," Lurie said. "You've got to show clinical benefit in humans: Does it work?" Peptide promoters lean on anecdotes, often without verifiable numbers. In a podcast recorded at the White House, the MAHA influencer Brecka said: "Twenty million people have been prescribed these things without adverse events." His guest on the episode, Brigham Buhler - the co-author of "The Peptide Revolution" and owner of a compounding pharmacy that sells peptides and a clinic, Ways2Well, that prescribes them - told Brecka that none of its 75,000-plus patients had reported adverse events from peptides. Buhler cited even higher numbers in the movie "MAHA Uncensored," a documentary featuring Kennedy and other leaders of the MAHA movement, and that bears the MAHA trademark. In the segment on peptides, Buhler said, "Having treated literally hundreds of thousands of people through our compounding pharmacy, we've never had a major adverse event." Topol asks why those boasting success haven't conducted clinical studies. "If influencers and companies really believe these peptides are helping people," Topol said, "then they should put their profits back into rigorous research." Chris Woodward, a spokesperson for Brecka and his company, the Ultimate Human, said in an email that the health and wellness issues discussed on Brecka's podcast do not constitute medical advice. "Mr. Brecka consistently advises his audience to consult a licensed physician," Woodward wrote. Buhler did not respond to requests for comment. Not all anecdotes are rosy. At an antiaging conference in July 2025 Las Vegas, two women were rushed to the hospital and intubated after being injected with experimental peptides and vitamins at a booth in the exhibit hall, according to citations that Nevada's state pharmacy board issued against the doctor running the booth and his colleagues for prescribing and administering drugs without a state medical license. An FDA database for adverse events contains concerning reports. Although the database can't prove that a drug, vaccine or medical device caused harm - the reports are brief, unverified and voluntary - it signals issues worth exploring. A 36-year-old woman was hospitalized in December after taking BPC-157 for weight control and a skin disorder, for example, and a 48-year-old man was hospitalized with a "life-threatening" condition after taking the peptide. FDA scientists presented some of these reports at the July meeting and flagged worrisome outcomes in animal experiments, such as a 2020 study revealing signs of liver toxicity in rats and dogs injected with BPC-157. Brian Lee, a liver disease specialist at the University of Southern California, was among the panel's minority who voted against easing restrictions. Without clinical studies, he said, afflictions that take time to develop, like liver damage and cancer, might not be spotted for years: "I think this endorsement can be potentially harmful, and I cannot in good conscience vote yes." The panel's newcomers disagreed. "I do not believe the FDA made a good case on issues with safety with BPC," said Kris Wusterhausen, founder of an antiaging company in Texas, the Resurge Clinic, which sells a BPC-157 product for $149. "Once you've seen the effects of BPC," he said, "you can't unsee it." Awaiting trial Deepak Srivastava, president of the Gladstone Institutes in San Francisco, designed a clinical trial two decades ago to see if a peptide he studies, TB-4, could repair tissue after a heart attack. Before enrollment, people volunteering for the study would be screened for early signs of cancer because TB-4 triggers vessel growth and cell migration, which might exacerbate malignant growths. He worries about the FDA panel's vote to ease restrictions on a derivative of TB-4, before such trials have been completed, saying, "You need to have a healthy respect for the fact that drugs can be harmful." Pinchas Cohen, a peptide researcher at the University of Southern California, was less cautious, saying the FDA buzz might drive investors to fund trials. He's seeking support to bring a peptide his lab identified, MOTS-c, to market. It's "un-ideal" for people to take unproven drugs, Cohen said, but that's what's happening: "The world is changing, and people like me need to accept that this is the new reality and find ways to make it as safe as possible." In the meantime, people like Meetze resort to podcasts and online forums for advice. His symptoms faded after a year, but he still had spells of feeling "zero emotions." Peptide users describe this condition as anhedonia. It's come up on Huberman's podcasts. Huberman occasionally mentions other potential peptide risks, like cancer, sprinkling them into advice on how to take them. Take a 2024 episode with 1.2 million views: "I do not think that BPC-157 is not without its quote-unquote 'side effects,'" Huberman says. He adds, "If you're going to go down this path of taking BPC-157, I would encourage you to take the minimal effective dose, to not simply do it every day, and certainly to not do it continuously, and of course to monitor your other health metrics for anything that could potentially resemble cancer or tumor growth, because obviously stimulating angiogenesis for wound repair sounds like a great thing - recovering and being able to do your workouts or play your sport, or move about more comfortably, of course - a wonderfully attractive thing to do." "Isn't that what we all want? But obviously not with the trade-off of growing a tumor," he said, before interrupting the discussion to advertise a supplement company sponsoring the show. item.title: Many GOP lawmakers are losing faith in the party's lame-duck ambitions
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Republicans have had to defer many of their legislative dreams, hoping the post-election release of political pressure could set up a productive “lame duck” session before a new Congress is seated. Fat chance, many GOP lawmakers now say. Beyond the uncertainties surrounding the midterms and a potential transition of power on Capitol Hill, members will return to Washington facing a considerable list of must-pass bipartisan bills but also potentially messy internal leadership fights, a foul national mood and a mere 24 legislative days to get anything done. One thing on Republicans’ minds is whether some of their members even come back to vote . “The question becomes: Who shows up for work after the elections?” Rep. Austin Scott (R-Ga.) said in an interview. “Attendance is an issue right now.” There are some items, Scott added, that “ultimately … have to get done.” Those include an extension of government funding past Dec. 11 and the annual Pentagon policy bill. Major pieces of legislation to reauthorize farm, transportation and surveillance programs are also on deck . All are loaded with potential partisan flash points, however, and won’t be legislative chip shots. Then there are pending bipartisan bills overhauling energy permitting and the college sports industry that many members are itching to get done this year. But many lawmakers fear those could easily get left behind — especially if Democrats can win control of either chamber and seek greater influence on the final products. “What do you think?” an exasperated Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said about the prospect for bipartisan accomplishments in the lame duck. “I mean, why? If you think about it, if Democrats win the House, why would they?” Rep. Dan Newhouse (R-Wash.), who like Tillis is leaving Congress at the end of the year, echoed the belief that Democrats would “want to put their fingerprints more on things before they pass” in a majority-flips scenario. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer suggested as much in a recent interview : “The lame duck will be quite different if we win the Senate,” he said. “Same thing if they win the House, and same thing if we win both or neither.” Then there are partisan GOP priorities that some Republicans are hoping to ram through in the final weeks of the year — especially if the party’s governing trifecta is about to end — such as enacting hundreds of millions of dollars in new defense funding as well as new voting restrictions. While GOP leaders are leaving the door open to attempting to pass another bill through the party-line reconciliation process, there are no signs they are closer to having the necessary votes than they were this summer. While some Republicans believe that losing a chamber would jump-start that process, others privately believe the exact opposite would happen, according to three GOP aides granted anonymity to speak candidly. There will be little incentive for lawmakers who just lost their seats — “free-range chickens,” some call them — to grind out a final legislative win, if they come back at all. Senate Majority Leader John Thune last month admitted he is facing mathematical realities that make passing another reconciliation bill “difficult” even in a lame-duck session. That likely spells doom for another GOP wish being bandied about for the post-midterms session: clearing a debt-limit increase through the end of President Donald Trump’s term. Thune has acknowledged that as a possibility multiple times since July, but several GOP senators are skeptical. “I don't like that idea,” said retiring Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.), who added she had to “hold my nose” in voting for the last debt-ceiling lift. But other GOP leaders are professing more optimism about the post-midterm environment to overcome some long-standing roadblocks. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise in an interview called it “an opportunity for everybody to focus on getting policy done because the election will be over.” “I hope we get back to that, because it needs to happen,” he said. But each piece of legislation still in limbo is riddled with thorny policy disputes. Senate Democrats blocked the defense bill amid a standoff over the Iran war and have objected to giving Trump back some surveillance powers. The farm bill, meanwhile, is mired in a fight over food assistance . Thune has teed up an initial vote on the bipartisan permitting deal , but Democrats continue to doubt whether Trump will live up to GOP negotiators’ clean energy commitments — and they could push for more concessions if they prevail in the midterms. Even the must-do government funding bill is a potential minefield, with lawmakers widely expecting a punt until deeper into the holidays or even next year. Democrats are fuming over the Trump administration’s recent decision to block roughly $1 billion in congressionally approved funding, which could complicate the dealmaking ahead of the deadline. That could make passage of the 12 annual spending bills, or a combined full-year “omnibus” package, impossible. “I just don't think we'll get them done by the 11th,” Rep. Mike Simpson of Idaho, a senior GOP appropriator, said about the full-year bills. He predicted another short-term punt. Beyond the policy disputes, there’s a host of other distractions leaders of both parties will be dealing with once they return to session Nov. 9. Speaker Mike Johnson will immediately have to deal with a House vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth forced by outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.). With the Iran war weighing heavily on voters’ views of the GOP, some Republicans with an eye on the next election could decide to break ranks. And though the elections will be over outside the Capitol, internal politicking could continue for weeks in both chambers. A Democratic flip of the House could spark a potentially chaotic cascade of GOP leadership elections, especially with Johnson giving mixed signals about his intentions in that scenario. He broached the possibility he might not remain atop his conference in a Fox News interview last week, then said in a CBS News interview published Monday that he expected "my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference" even after a loss. Thune says he is running again for GOP leader regardless of the election outcome, and no other senator has signaled they will challenge him. That hasn’t stopped some conservatives, in and out of the chamber, from questioning whether Trump will blame him if the majority is lost. Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said the lame duck to-do list could ultimately come down to vibes. “I know what they would like us to do and all that,” Kennedy said. “But you have no idea what the mood is going to be.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/13/gop-lame-duck-reality-check-01114594

item.title: Trump faces a tough choice after Houthi attacks kill an American in Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
London — Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have dramatically upped the stakes in the complex Middle East war, killing at least 20 people — including an American — and wounding hundreds more with strikes on Saudi Arabia's airports over the last week. The question is whether President Trump will order U.S. military action in support of Saudi Arabia, which has been at war with the rebels in Yemen for more than a decade. Mr. Trump campaigned on ending wars, and he is likely aware, less than a month before the U.S. midterm elections, that opening a new U.S. front in the wider conflict sparked by the Feb. 28 joint U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran could be politically perilous. If he did, he could argue that it is both to protect the Saudis, as a key U.S. ally, and to stop the Iranian proxy group from threatening global shipping in the vital trade routes of the Red Sea. Mr. Trump rejected a request last month by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to join in the kingdom's strikes on the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News . He came close to ordering airstrikes against the group a week later , but again declined. Asked Sunday if the U.S. would join Saudi strikes, however, the president replied: "We may. We're gonna look at it … We'll make a decision. We move very quickly." So, what has changed, and will it be enough to force Mr. Trump's hand? An American death Little information has come out about the U.S. citizen killed in the Saturday attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, but the killing of an American may increase pressure on Mr. Trump to retaliate. According to Nadwa al-Dawsari, associate fellow at the Middle East Institute, it may not be enough in itself, however, to spur the president to further entrench the U.S. in the wider regional conflict. "I don't think that the killing of an American will trigger a military response," she told CBS News on Monday. "The Houthis have killed American civilians before, including detainees who died after being tortured by the Houthis in Sanaa , and that did not provoke a response from the U.S., militarily or otherwise. Trump's decision will likely depend on his broader assessment of the risks of further escalation." Oil prices Oil prices may be one of the biggest factors in the president's calculus. He has vowed repeatedly to bring down prices at the pump , which have soared as a result of the war with Iran impeding exports from major Persian Gulf energy producers. The Trump administration insists Iran has no control over the Strait of Hormuz, and more oil has been getting out of the Middle East from the Persian Gulf in recent weeks. But the Houthis hold significant territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast, which has enabled them to threaten vessels there and in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and another key chokepoint for global energy supplies. If the Houthis are able to control Yemen's coastline, or enough of it to maintain their threat to shipping via the Bab el-Mandeb, it would put more pressure on energy flows, increasing the leverage Iran and its proxy groups have over global fuel prices. Thomas Juneau, associate fellow at the Chatham House think tank's Middle East and North Africa Program, told CBS News that this creates "a difficult dilemma for President Trump." "Direct U.S. involvement would likely lead to greater tension in the Red Sea, and therefore create more upward pressure on oil prices," he said. "Should the U.S. refuse to become directly engaged, however, it will cause growing resentment and anger in Saudi Arabia, where feelings of abandonment caused by a widespread perception that the U.S. is failing to support its partner at a time of need are already acute." Helping an ally Despite long-running U.S. accusations that some members of the Saudi leadership supported the al Qaeda Sept. 11 hijackers , and the fallout from the brutal murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018, Saudi Arabia has managed to maneuver itself into a position of relative international respectability over the last few years, pursuing a raft of economic reforms to attract foreign investment and building on its status as the world's top oil exporter. The foreign money and visitors could dry up, however, if the Saudis prove incapable of defending themselves from Houthi attacks. Saudi authorities regularly report intercepting Houthi weapons . But the death toll over the last week has exposed gaping holes in Saudi defenses. The Reuters news agency reported Tuesday that the Saudi system to warn civilians of a military attack went silent days before the latest series of deadly Houthi strikes. The Trump administration has fostered close business and defense ties with the Saudis , and failing to come to the aid of an ally in need — especially one that hosts five U.S. military bases — could make Washington appear to be an unreliable ally. What do the Saudis want, and would it be effective? Of all the military options at Mr. Trump's disposal, airstrikes on Houthi targets "would make the greatest difference," al-Dawsari told CBS News. The U.S. has, so far, only acknowledged offering intelligence and targeting support to Saudi Arabia. "The United States can also strengthen air and missile defense cooperation and help identify Houthi launch sites, weapons facilities, and command-and-control infrastructure," al-Dawsari said. While the aim of U.S. strikes would likely be "to degrade the Houthis' ability to launch missiles and drones against Saudi Arabia and threaten shipping in the Red Sea," al-Dawsari said "airstrikes alone will not eliminate the Houthi threat." "The real question is whether American military action would be part of a broader effort to weaken the Houthis, or simply another round of limited strikes that they can absorb and recover from," she said. "The risk is that the United States becomes drawn into a prolonged military campaign against the Houthis while already fighting Iran. But there is also a risk in allowing the Houthis to continue operating as an Iranian military asset and a threat in their own right at Bab el-Mandeb and in the Red Sea," she added. "The United States has a significant interest in keeping the Bab el-Mandeb open, and in protecting the Saudi economy — in particular, the kingdom's ability to export energy products," said CBS News national security analyst Aaron MacLean. "A world in which the Houthis are regularly scoring spectacular hits in Saudi Arabia … is not a world in which America's interests are secure." MacLean cautioned, however, that in addition to the risk of making energy markets even more nervous and driving prices up further, "President Trump has to consider that American military action targeting the Houthis will almost certainly be indecisive." While U.S. strikes could help push the Houthis back and reduce their attack capabilities for a time, "the most Washington can reasonably hope for from a major military operation — adding American airpower to existing capabilities on the ground — is a 'mowing of the lawn,'" said MacLean, and "participating in a protracted conflict with no clear theory of how to end it is a tough sell when you are a president who campaigned on ending so-called 'endless wars.'" The U.S. has targeted the Houthis before , with strikes between March and May 2025 to prevent the group from attacking commercial ships in the Red Sea . The group claimed those attacks were in support of Palestinians, amid Israel's blockade of the Gaza Strip. The U.S. strikes did "cause significant pain to the Houthis … much more than what Saudi Arabia has been able to do," said Juneau, at Chatham House in London. But even those American strikes "were not sufficient to fully deter the Houthis from continuing their attacks in the Red Sea, let alone to defeat them," he said. "The bar for President Trump to authorize strikes now is seemingly pretty high," according to Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. "The U.S. is only likely to intercede now in the event of a Houthi attack that results in several U.S. casualties." Asked about the Houthis, President Trump said Monday that the rebels were "misbehaving very badly." He repeated that in a Truth Social post Tuesday, adding that he thought the group "learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed the HELL out of them." "Now they've emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran," Mr. Trump said in the post, adding that the rebels were "in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections — NOT NICE. Somebody should explain to them that I'm not running in the Elections, I've already won, IN A MASSIVE LANDSLIDE, but I'll be there after the Elections, and I will never forget!" In an interview with the French news agency AFP, meanwhile, Houthi political bureau member Mohammed al-Bukhaiti warned Tuesday that if the U.S. chooses to get "involved in the aggression against Yemen, we will not deliberate over the decision to respond, rather, there will be a swift and painful response targeting the U.S. and all its interests in the region." Given the Pentagon's recent acknowledgment of U.S. munitions shortages caused by the war with Iran, Mr. Trump will have to consider carefully the American military's ability to defend against and respond to potential Houthi retaliatory attacks if he does wade into Yemen's civil war. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/iran-war-houthis-saudi-arabia-trump-faces-difficult-dilemma/

item.title: Elon Musk's megaphone propels conspiracy theory about James Talarico
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Elon Musk elevated a false conspiracy theory about Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico over the weekend, lifting a fringe claim concerning the Texan’s mental health to the forefront of users’ X feeds, where it garnered hundreds of thousands of impressions. “The Talarico campaign is hiding something big that voters ought to know about,” Musk wrote Sunday afternoon, replying to a post alleging that Talarico had been checked into the Lindner Center of Hope, a mental health facility in suburban Cincinnati. Musk’s reply amassed over 870,000 views, more than double the impression count of the post to which he was responding. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The theory had been circulating online for days, fueled by Talarico’s absence from the campaign trail, which his team has consistently said was due to the flu. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton promoted a “Tala-Freak-Out Tip Line” on Friday, which was still active as of Monday night. President Donald Trump weighed in, arguing the Democrat’s convalescence was too long to be the “flu bug.” Musk’s engagement with the theory gave it a much wider audience - and the flurry of attention ultimately prompted the treatment center in Mason, Ohio, to publicly refute the allegations. “Rep. James Talarico has never received treatment from Lindner Center of Hope,” the facility wrote in a statement posted to X, five hours after Musk’s initial posts on the subject. Talarico replied to the post Monday, saying he had “never even been to Ohio,” with a laughing emoji. A day earlier, he described the conspiracy theory as “the craziest thing I’ve ever heard” in an interview with MS NOW. Talarico’s spokesperson, JT Ennis, said the claims were a “lie designed to promote a pathetic conspiracy theory.” The episode demonstrates a key way that Musk is wielding political power in the midterms. He has retreated from the political spotlight after his public feud with Trump in 2025. He has taken a lower-profile approach to political spending this election cycle. He has used his formidable war chest to quietly back efforts to elect Republicans to office. The New York Times reported on Monday his midterm spending has swelled to at least $276 million since the beginning of July, making him the Republicans’ top individual donor. But on X, the social media platform he bought in 2022 and later folded into SpaceX, Musk continues to be outspoken about candidates and political issues - and his enormous audience acts as an influence machine, propelling a fringe claim into the political conversation with a single post. “You have someone … who is in bed with the political party, or an agenda, and is spreading falsehoods about an opponent who is gaining a tremendous amount of traction,” said Danielle Citron, a University of Virginia law professor who has spent more than a decade researching and writing about online abuse and has advised campaigns on the subject. “It is like a thumb on the scale that we haven’t really ever seen.” The Lindner Center of Hope and Musk did not respond to requests for comment. The theory surrounding Talarico originated in far-right circles, spreading further when right-wing influencer Nick Sortor posted an audio clip. The clip, which he claimed was a clinic employee stating that Talarico had recently been discharged, received 7.3 million views according to X. Sortor called for the Texas Democrat to quit the race. Talarico’s campaign said the candidate had been recovering from the flu, leading to a nine-day absence from the campaign trail. He appeared at an Austin music festival on Friday, even though the call that Sortor posted was recorded on Saturday night, according to phone logs posted by the caller. The conspiracy theories drove mentions of Talarico among key right-wing figures - including politicians and influencers - to their highest rate on record, a Washington Post analysis found. Until last week, Musk had posted relatively infrequently on Talarico - just twice in the past year. Since Wednesday, however, Musk has posted about Talarico at least a dozen times. One of Musk’s posts Sunday, a repost to his more than 240 million followers, put the onus on Talarico to clear the record: “If this was not true, Talarico’s campaign would immediately authorize the release of the records to clear him.” While Sortor’s audio clip led discussion to peak between 1 and 2 p.m. on Sunday, Musk weighed in as the matter was driving a significant level of conversation in right-wing circles - and it continued to hold traction for about eight hours afterward. Jared Holt, a senior researcher at Open Measures, a platform that measures the spread of online extremism and disinformation, said Musk’s elevation helped claims like Sortor’s proliferate. “His engagement with posts promoting the claims did boost them to wider audiences than they may have reached otherwise and likely served to legitimize them in the eyes of ideologically aligned users,” Holt said in an email. This kind of public attention can prove dangerous for ordinary figures suddenly lifted to the center of public fascination, he added. “The ecosystem where these claims spread has regularly elicited threats to schools, medical facilities, election offices, courts, and private businesses,” Holt said. Since buying the site formerly known as Twitter in 2022, Musk has regularly injected high-profile misinformation into users’ feeds. Late last year, Musk elevated allegations that members of the Somali-American community were involved in widespread fraud. Some rogue X users followed the posts from participants in the fraud claims to real life locations. Musk has also spread baseless theories about a volunteer in a Thai cave rescue, California wildfires and other topics. In 2022, shortly after acquiring Twitter, Musk elevated a conspiracy theory about Paul Pelosi, the husband of former Democratic House speaker Nancy Pelosi, who was badly injured in an attack at the family’s San Francisco home after a hammer-wielding intruder broke in and struck him in the head repeatedly. The rapid spread of online theories can place political campaigns in a tricky situation. Zac Petkanas was Hillary Clinton’s rapid response director during 2016 campaign, when online conspiracy theories alleged Clinton was secretly seriously ill and had to employ a body double to replace her on the campaign trail. “The way that it mattered [to Clinton’s campaign] was not that people believed Pizzagate or other conspiracy theories; it’s that it contributed to a narrative that she was potentially untrustworthy,” Petkanas said. “It was sort of a death by 1,000 paper cuts, and that was partly because people were really having to judge information coming off of the internet and realizing the scale at which misinformation could be weaponized. It’s 10 years later. People are much more inured to that.” Citron, the University of Virginia law professor, said actors take advantage of the short windows between campaigns and elections to spread falsehoods because they are unlikely to face consequences. If a claim is defamatory, for example, she said, the matter can take too long to resolve in the courts to have an impact on the race. “Given we’re within 30 days of an election, I think your lawsuit is not doing anything for you,” she said. “They know they’re in that chokepoint where you can tip an election. … It’s timed just right.” - - - Graphics: Right-wing attention on Talarico spiked on Sunday Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/13/fringe-theory-about-james-talarico-went-viral-then-elon-musk-weighed/

item.title: Zelensky says Ukraine received no early warning from partners about missiles headed to Kyiv
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine received no early warning from its partners about five Russian ballistic missiles that hit civilian infrastructure in the capital of Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday, as tensions rise between the Ukrainian leader and U.S. President Donald Trump. Zelenskyy did not specify which partners he was talking about. He characterized the barrage as “particularly vile” and emphasized that receiving intelligence from partners about such attacks “helps save lives" and is "one of the most critical issues.” "This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed — when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he wrote in a post on X. Trump said the U.S. has not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “We want the war to end, so we’re working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end." More missiles struck Kyiv late Tuesday, targeting energy systems. Zelenskyy said again that the country received no early warning from partners. “It is important that the world does not stay silent about this,” he posted on X. “And it is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing.” Remarks follow biting criticism from Trump Zelenskyy’s remarks come days after Trump unleashed biting criticism of him, including comments that it was time for a new president in Ukraine and that Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war. The criticism marks perhaps the lowest point in their relationship since their disastrous Oval Office meeting in February 2025. Kyiv continues to rely heavily on Washington for military assistance, including U.S.-made Patriot missile-defense systems and intelligence. The U.S. has the capability to immediately spot Russian ballistic missile launches. American officials have in the past notified Ukraine about launches to allow it to issue missile warnings to the public and to use air defenses against incoming missiles. Asked whether Ukraine received an explanation for the lack of intelligence ahead of the overnight missile strikes, a senior Ukrainian official said it was described as a “failure,” suggesting it was the result of circumstances such as weather conditions rather than a deliberate decision. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to give an official statement on the matter. Ukraine struggles to fend off aerial attacks Russia's war in Ukraine has not seen major shifts on the ground since last year, but Ukraine is struggling to fend off Moscow's intensified aerial attacks that include speedy ballistic missiles and high-flying jet-powered drones . Downing the missiles has been a challenge because of a shortage of Patriot missiles caused by the U.S.-led war in Iran. Russia’s Iskander short-range ballistic missiles take just a few minutes to reach targets in Ukraine. Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 100 weapons since Monday evening. A residential building in the northeastern city of Kharkiv was destroyed, killing four people despite an all-night rescue operation, he said. Russia has increasingly used attacks on civilian infrastructure such as energy facilities to deny Ukrainians power, heat and running water during the 4½-year war, hoping to wear down public support for Ukraine’s response to Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Zelenskyy says Ukraine is respecting energy ceasefire Trump has blamed Ukraine's earlier strikes on Russian oil refineries for record U.S. diesel prices — rather than the war in Iran . He struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday to import diesel from Russia in an attempt to bring fuel prices down ahead of U.S. midterm elections. Meanwhile, Trump claimed Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed on an “energy ceasefire” in which both parties would refrain from striking each other's energy infrastructure. Russia has not confirmed the existence of such a deal. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said only that “contacts on this matter continue.” Zelenskyy on Tuesday said Ukraine had not struck Russian oil refineries or other energy sites in the two days since Trump announced the purported deal. He criticized Moscow for what he said were Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities and infrastructure in the time since Trump's announcement. “The facts show that the Russians do not consider themselves bound by what the President of the United States said,” Zelenskyy said following the attack late Tuesday. The claim that Ukraine has halted its strikes on energy sites could not be independently verified, but neither Russian officials nor media have reported Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries since the energy truce was announced. Strikes on Kharkiv kill 4 and wound 41 Russian strikes across Ukraine caused injuries and deaths overnight Monday and into Tuesday. In addition to the four deaths in the apartment building in Kharkiv, 41 people were wounded in the city in one evening alone, Zelenskyy said. A woman was wounded in a Russian strike on a private home in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district, the Kyiv city military administration said. A Russian drone hit a residential building in the village of Murovane, near the western city of Lviv, during a morning attack Tuesday, Lviv Mayor Andrii Sadovyi said. One person was killed in the Fastiv district of the Kyiv region, and at least two others were hurt in a Russian attack on the area, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration. A Russian drone struck an educational institution in the center of Rivne in northwest Ukraine, wounding 14 people, according to Oleksandr Koval, head of the Rivne regional military administration. The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement Tuesday that its forces launched strikes "against Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, logistics centers, railway and port infrastructure, as well as vessels involved in delivering military cargo to Ukraine.” The ministry also said a bulk carrier headed to the port of Mykolaiv with military cargo on board was hit in the estuary of the Bug River along the Black Sea. The Russian Defense Ministry on Tuesday said its air defenses overnight shot down 604 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions and the Sea of Azov. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 417 drones targeted the Moscow region. Most were downed far away, while 65 were intercepted as they approached the Russian capital. A school, two private houses and a car were damaged in the attack in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow, Gov. item.description:

President Trump has begun to downplay his new deal with Russia after a plan to allow imports of Russian diesel into the US came under withering criticism, even from members of his own party. "It's a deal for the world ... It's not a deal with me," Trump told reporters on Tuesday morning, repeating that it was "not a USA deal." "They're releasing it to the entire world," Trump added, after making similar comments on Monday that the deal would help US farmers, but said, "It's not really a deal with me, it's a deal for the rest of the world." President Trump speaks to members of the media as he departs the White House on Oct. 13 to travel to Alaska for a rally. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images) Chip Somodevilla via Getty Images The contention is a marked shift since Trump announced the plans last week. "I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia," he wrote on Truth Social , adding that it will be a "great announcement...for Americans and, indeed, the World." The deal will include a quick release of 300,000 tons (about 2.2 million barrels) of diesel. That would then be followed by another 500,000 in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter" for a total of about 13.5 million barrels. His administration quickly authorized US purchases of Russian diesel through next April. Calls on the president to 'immediately reverse course' Blowback to the plan has been notable — even within Trump's own party. A bipartisan group of senators called on the president to "immediately reverse course," in a letter signed by Republican Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and John Curtis of Utah, along with three Democrats. The plan has also received a lukewarm reception on the midterm campaign trail, with figures like Republican Mike Rogers, who is locked in a tight Senate contest in Michigan, distancing himself from it . Some energy experts suggest the deal might run afoul of US law, while others suggest it simply won't work since Russia seems to lack enough excess diesel refining capacity to markedly increase exports and move US or global diesel prices. Read more: How oil price shocks ripple through your wallet, from gas to groceries In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin is seen in Moscow on Oct. 11. (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool/AFP via Getty Images) VYACHESLAV PROKOFYEV via Getty Images Indeed, the current average price of diesel, according to the American Automobile Association, was almost $6.28 per gallon on Tuesday, a tick up from almost $6.27 per gallon on Monday. Wholesale diesel prices are "not blinking over Russia/US 'deal'" Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, noted on Tuesday . "Truckers and farmers not going to see any relief anytime soon." But Trump continued to defend the deal and dodged a question about another major critique, which is that it could fund Russia's war efforts against Ukraine. "Nobody's told me anything," the president said Tuesday in response to whether Russia could use any of the funds to further attack Ukraine. Trump also claimed without evidence that the deal had brought down prices and reaffirmed that his larger goal was to end the overall conflict. He said of Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, "I think they both want it to end, you know, honestly, they both want it to end, and they don't know how to get to that point." item.title: Duane 'Keffe D' Davis gets 40 years to life for orchestrating Tupac Shakur’s killing
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Jack Queen and Steve Gorman LAS VEGAS, Oct 13 (Reuters) - A former gang leader was sentenced to 40 years to life in prison on Tuesday for orchestrating the 1996 drive-by shooting death of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas, capping the prosecution of a long-unsolved ‌murder that shaped the golden age of rap music. Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, found guilty of first-degree murder in August, received the sentence during a hearing ‌in a Las Vegas courtroom. In tearful testimony before Judge Carli Kierny, Shakur's younger sister Sekyiwa Shakur said their mother had raised him to be a human rights activist and treated him as if he ​had the potential to change the world. "He believed her," said Sekyiwa Shakur, wearing a black shirt. "He went out in the world to do that. And I believe he would have done it." Until Davis' 2023 arrest, the killing of Shakur, shot dead in the passenger seat of an SUV driven by his record executive, Marion "Suge" Knight, had stood for nearly three decades as one of America's most notorious cold cases. The murder, which silenced one of rap's most commercially successful and influential artists, heightened the image of violence permeating 1990s hip-hop culture ‌while stoking the infamous East Coast-West Coast "gangsta" rap feud ⁠of the era. Despite Davis' conviction, the question of who pulled the trigger in the fatal shooting of the 25-year-old rap legend has never been conclusively decided. Davis was tried and convicted for masterminding the murder to avenge the beating of his nephew by Shakur and ⁠members of the rapper's entourage inside the MGM Grand casino on the Las Vegas Strip on September 7, 1996. Davis has said he would appeal his conviction. 'THE WORLD NEVER FORGOT' Authorities said they long believed Davis was involved in Shakur's killing but lacked sufficient evidence to charge him. That changed when he went public with his story in media appearances and a memoir that, along ​with ​tapes of his secret meetings with investigators, formed the bulk of the prosecution’s murder case. In his ​book, "Compton Street Legend," Davis himself wrote that he was considered a ‌suspect in the murders of both Shakur and Christopher Wallace, a rival rapper. Addressing Davis on Tuesday, Kierny said his assertions that he had changed since the 1990s fell short. "You don't get to take a man from his family," Kierny said, referring to Shakur. "The world never forgot about him." FATAL SHOOTING SPARKED BY CASINO BRAWL The clash at the casino stemmed from hostility between two Los Angeles-area street gangs — the South Side Compton Crips, of which Davis was the self-described leader, and Mob Piru, which was associated with Shakur, Knight, and their music label, Death Row Records. Members of both groups were in Las Vegas to see a world heavyweight title boxing match that night between Mike ‌Tyson and Bruce Seldon. Within hours of the casino brawl, Davis ushered his nephew and two ​other associates into a white Cadillac and went looking for Shakur and Knight, determined to settle scores, ​according to an account Davis later gave police in an unrelated investigation ​and that prosecutors cited during his murder trial. Davis said he passed a gun to the two men seated behind him in the ‌Cadillac, one of whom opened fire through the window when they ​caught up with, and pulled alongside of, ​Knight and Shakur’s vehicle in traffic. Shakur was struck four times and died in a hospital six days later. Knight, who suffered a minor injury from a bullet fragment that grazed his head, is now serving a 28-year prison term on an unrelated voluntary manslaughter conviction. While Davis was never accused of actually ​firing the shots that killed Shakur - Nevada law allows someone ‌to be charged with murder as a participant in the crime - prosecutors have never named a suspected gunman. All three other men in the Cadillac ​with Davis that night have since died. item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Officials are reviewing the off-base code of conduct for U.S. troops in Japan following the killing of an Okinawan woman, allegedly by a U.S. Marine , Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said on Tuesday. Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-runs and drunk driving by U.S. military personnel have long triggered protests on the southern Japanese island, which has for years urged other regions of the country to share the burden of hosting U.S. troops. "We plan to hold discussions including whether the existing rules are effectively functioning," Motegi said, adding that "matters such as patrols and curfew management" would be under review in talks with the United States. The high-level bilateral consultations will examine off-duty conduct and the "liberty" policy governing off-base private activities of U.S. military personnel, he said. The existing policy, updated in 2024 following a string of sexual assaults by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa, includes a ban on them drinking in public off-base between 1 a.m. and 5 a.m. or going to bars during those hours. Japanese police arrested a U.S. Marine stationed on Okinawa early this month on suspicion of killing a 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa Orefecture. Word of the arrest drew outrage . The U.S. military enacted a two-day operational pause after the Marine's arrest to reinforce discipline and standards, followed by a monthlong midnight-to-5 a.m. curfew. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Tuesday that "we began high-level, working-level consultations between Japan and the United States last week on what effective measures should be taken." "The Japanese government will continue to do everything in its power both to address this case and to ensure that it does not happen again," she told a legislative committee session. Motegi spoke by phone over the weekend with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who offered his "sincere condolences" over the alleged crime and pledged U.S. cooperation in the investigation. Crimes committed by U.S. personnel have long been a thorn in relations between the close security allies. A Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison last year . In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa. The United States has approximately 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
